extracted.intended_audience: writers, playwrights, critics and students of comic theory / literary humorists
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts practical, formal and psychological principles that define comic effects (forms, situations, devices) useful for playwrights, humorists and critics analyzing or composing comedy. Emphasises mechanisms (mechanisation of life), playful devices, and three formal methods of light comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: We laugh every time a person gives us the impression of being a thing.
rubrics_metrics.description: WE LAUGH EVERY TIME A PERSON GIVES US THE IMPRESSION OF BEING A THING.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation and examples: Sancho Panza tumbled into a bed-quilt, Baron Munchausen as a cannon-ball, circus-clown routines where performers become rounder and more like balls or wooden dummies. The comic arises when human flesh-and-blood is perceived as an object or mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradual passing from the dim and vague to the clear (method of suggestion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consequently, the gradual passing from the dim and vague to the clear and distinct is the method of suggestion par excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to induce hallucinated images or comic transformations by degrees (hypnotist example, falling-asleep imagery). Poetic devices (rhythm, rhyme, assonance) can lull imagination into accepting a suggested image (examples: lines of Regnard; Figaro's rapid stringing of adjectives suggesting a doll or an animal). This method underlies coarse and subtle comic suggestions alike.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talking about persons as mere things
rubrics_metrics.description: All those that can be obtained by talking about persons as one would do about mere things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic effects can be built by treating persons impersonally or confusing person with function (e.g., M. Perrichon's parcel count turning wife/daughter/self into numbered items; village mayor confusing prefect's identity with office). Identification need not be complete; partial confusion (person vs. function) suffices if it fits the mental state or circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: comic situation = illusion of life + impression of mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: ANY ARRANGEMENT OF ACTS AND EVENTS IS COMIC WHICH GIVES US, IN A SINGLE COMBINATION, THE ILLUSION OF LIFE AND THE DISTINCT IMPRESSION OF A MECHANICAL ARRANGEMENT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a formal criterion for situations: comedy results when a dramatic sequence simultaneously suggests living continuity and, at the same time, the visible presence of a mechanical arrangement (strings, springs, gears). Examples: child's puppets grown human, characters who oscillate mechanically between states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jack-in-the-box / Repetition as comic mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: The Jack-in-the-box image: a spring bent and released repeatedly — leading to the comic principle of REPETITION.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repetition on stage (words or actions) is comic not in itself but because it symbolizes two moral elements: a repressed feeling that bursts like a spring and an idea that delights in repressing it. Examples: Punch and Judy policeman, Sganarelle vs Pancrace, Monsieur Purgon/Argan, Dorine and Orgon's repeated 'Et Tartuffe?', Scapin playing on Geronte's avarice, Harpagon's repeated 'No dowry wanted!'. The mechanical automatism of repetition produces the jack-in-the-box effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dancing-jack / Characters manipulated like toys
rubrics_metrics.description: There are innumerable comedies in which one of the characters thinks he is speaking and acting freely ... whereas, viewed from a certain standpoint, he appears as a mere toy in the hands of another who is playing with him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: render a supposedly free character as visibly controlled by another (Scapin manipulating Geronte/Argante). The comic can also derive from personifying opposing decisions or impulses as separate actors (so that inner vacillation appears as external puppet-strings). Spectators often side with the manipulator; the image of strings/wires makes serious action comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Snow-ball (cumulative escalation / reversibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: The snow-ball: an effect which grows by arithmetical progression, so that the cause, insignificant at the outset, culminates by a necessary evolution in a result as important as it is unexpected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic device of cumulative causation (toy soldiers, house of cards, chain of accidents). Frequently used in stage comedy and humorous illustration: chained mishaps that escalate, often with a circular/reversible element (the ball returns to the starting point), heightening the joke. Examples: lawsuits within lawsuits (Plaideurs), Don Quixote inn scene, Labiche's hat-eaten-by-horse and other plays (La Cagnotte, Les Surprises du divorce). Note: mere disproportion between cause and effect is not itself comic unless it reveals a mechanical arrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic as absentmindedness / automatism of life
rubrics_metrics.description: The rigid mechanism which we occasionally detect, as a foreign body, in the living continuity of human affairs is of peculiar interest to us as being a kind of ABSENTMINDEDNESS on the part of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: the comic exposes inelasticity/automatism/absence of attention in persons or events; laughter functions socially to single out and repress this absentmindedness. This explains why we laugh at mechanical traits in human affairs and why detection of strings/springs provokes laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three formal methods of light comedy: repetition, inversion, reciprocal interference of series
rubrics_metrics.description: Life presents itself as evolution in time and complexity in space ... take the counterpart of each of these: we shall obtain three processes which might be called REPETITION, INVERSION, and RECIPROCAL INTERFERENCE OF SERIES.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General formal taxonomy: these three methods correspond to the mechanical counterparts of life's characteristics (continuity, irreversibility, individuality). Repetition is elaborated in the text; inversion and reciprocal interference are identified as the other fundamental modes by which comic arrangements are constructed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition of a situation across acts / groups
rubrics_metrics.description: In a comic repetition of situations, a combination of circumstances recurs several times in its original form within an ever-moving series; it is more laughable the more complex and naturally introduced the repeat is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Playwrightic technique: repeat the same scene or arrangement in different tempi or with different groups (masters then servants) to create comedic symmetry. Examples in Moliere: L'Ecole des femmes (three tempi of the same incident), L'Ecole des marts, L'Etourdi, George Dandin. The writer must reconcile complexity and naturalness of repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification of opposing decisions (to dramatize inner vacillation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic author is always careful to PERSONIFY the two opposing decisions. For, if there is no spectator, there must at all events be actors to hold the strings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: make an inner duel visible by assigning opposing impulses to distinct characters or by staging the vacillation so it looks like a puppet-play (example: Panurge asking Tom, Dick, and Harry about marriage). This externalization turns a psychological hesitation into a mechanical/puppet-like comic scene.
